claim: Old yeast cells lose chromosomes by partitioning them asymmetrically to their daughter cells together with the pre-existing (old) spindle pole body (SPB).
source: Here, we report that old yeast cells lose chromosomes by partitioning them asymmetrically to their daughter cells together with the pre-existing (old) spindle pole body (SPB, centrosome equivalent in yeast).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 1 and 2, where chromosome loss and asymmetric segregation were directly observed and quantified in aging yeast cells.

claim: Remodelling of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) and the displacement of its nuclear basket triggered asymmetric chromosome segregation events in old yeast cells.
source: Strikingly, remodelling of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) and the displacement of its nuclear basket triggered these asymmetric chromosome segregation events.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 3 and 5 showing that mutations affecting basket stability (mlp1Δ) promote chromosome loss, while preventing basket displacement (sgf73Δ, fob1Δ) suppresses it.

claim: Nuclear basket displacement caused unspliced pre-mRNAs to leak into the cytoplasm in old yeast cells.
source: Simultaneously, nuclear basket displacement caused unspliced pre-mRNAs to leak into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA FISH data in Figure 7A-B showing cytoplasmic localization of intronic sequences in old cells, and by the pre-mRNA translation reporter data in Figure 7D-F.

claim: Removing the introns of three genes involved in chromosome segregation (GLC7, MCM21, NBL1) was sufficient to fully suppress chromosome loss in old cells.
source: We show that removing the introns of three genes involved in chromosome segregation was sufficient to fully suppress chromosome loss in old cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4B-C showing that the 3xΔi mutation (removal of all three introns) nearly completely suppressed chromosome loss and anaphase missegregation in old cells.

claim: Promoting pre-mRNA leakage in young cells caused asymmetric chromosome partitioning and loss through the same three introns.
source: Promoting pre-mRNA leakage in young cells also caused asymmetric chromosome partitioning and loss through the same three introns.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 8 showing that hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells, which leak pre-mRNA, exhibit increased chromosome missegregation that is suppressed by removing the three introns.

claim: Basket displacement from NPCs and its consequences for pre-mRNA quality control are key triggers of aging phenotypes such as aneuploidy.
source: Therefore, we propose that basket displacement from NPCs and its consequences for pre-mRNA quality control are key triggers of aging phenotypes such as aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the experimental data showing the causal chain from basket displacement to pre-mRNA leakage to chromosome loss.

claim: The NPC is remodelled in aging across evolutionary lineages, as shown in fungi, worms, and mammals.
source: Importantly, the NPC is remodelled in aging across evolutionary lineages, as shown in fungi, worms, and mammals (Rempel et al., 2020; Meinema et al., 2022; Rempel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The most prominent change in the NPCs of old cells is the loss of their nuclear basket.
source: The most prominent change in the NPCs of old cells is the loss of their nuclear basket, which lies on the nucleoplasmic side of the NPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and is consistent with the experimental observations in this study.

claim: Nuclear basket loss is observed both in dividing cells and upon expression of the progeric variant of Lamin A, progerin.
source: Nuclear basket loss is observed both in dividing cells and upon expression of the progeric variant of Lamin A, progerin (Jin et al., 2019; Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TPR (Mlp1 and Mlp2 in S. cerevisiae) is the main structural component of the nuclear basket in mammals.
source: The protein TPR (Mlp1 and Mlp2 in S. cerevisiae) is the main structural component of the nuclear basket in mammals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NPC structure.

claim: The nuclear basket serves as a critical processing hub for mRNA export and nuclear retention of pre-mRNA, protein quality control, and gene regulation.
source: The nuclear basket serves as a critical processing hub for mRNA export and nuclear retention of pre-mRNA, protein quality control, and gene regulation (Møller et al., 2018; Bitterman et al., 2003; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Shcheprova et al., 2008; Baldi et al., 2017; Boveri, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Budding yeast undergoes replicative aging, during which the mother cell produces a finite number of daughter cells before dying.
source: Budding yeast undergoes replicative aging, during which the mother cell produces a finite number of daughter cells before dying (Jacobs et al., 1961).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast aging supported by citation.

claim: The yeast NPC is remodelled during replicative aging.
source: Importantly, several studies have emphasized that the yeast NPC is remodelled during replicative aging (Rempel et al., 2020; Meinema et al., 2022; Rempel et al., 2019), but the exact consequences of its reorganization are not fully understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Extrachromosomal DNA circles (eccDNAs) accumulate in the mother cell nucleus and are one of the key drivers of aging in budding yeast.
source: Extrachromosomal DNA circles (also called eccDNAs) accumulate in the mother cell nucleus and are one of the key drivers of aging in the budding yeast (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Jin et al., 2019; Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vast majority of extrachromosomal DNA circles (>99%) stems from the highly repetitive rDNA locus and are referred to as extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs).
source: The vast majority of these circles (>99%) stems from the highly repetitive rDNA locus and are referred to as extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ERCs are replicated in S-phase and retained in the mother cell at mitosis.
source: As the cell ages, these circles accumulate exponentially because they are replicated in S-phase and retained in the mother cell at mitosis (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Bitterman et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: By the end of their life, yeast cells contain about 1000 ERCs, which represents roughly the same amount of DNA as the rest of the genome.
source: By the end of their life, yeast cells contain about 1000 ERCs, which represents roughly the same amount of DNA as the rest of the genome (Bitterman et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ERC retention in the mother cell relies on their anchorage to NPCs via the acetyltransferase complex SAGA.
source: Importantly, their retention in the mother cell relies on their anchorage to NPCs via the acetyltransferase complex SAGA (Meinema et al., 2022; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPC-ERC units are confined to the mother part of the dividing nucleus by a lateral diffusion barrier forming in the nuclear envelope in the future plane of cleavage.
source: These NPC-ERC units are then confined to the mother part of the dividing nucleus by a lateral diffusion barrier forming in the nuclear envelope in the future plane of cleavage (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Shcheprova et al., 2008; Baldi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast cells undergo a closed mitosis, meaning that they keep their nuclear envelope intact throughout mitosis.
source: Yeast cells undergo a closed mitosis, meaning that they keep their nuclear envelope intact throughout mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: Anchorage of ERCs to NPCs results in the dissociation of their nuclear basket, which is a direct result of SAGA-driven acetylation of nucleoporins on the nucleoplasmic side of the NPC, including Nup60.
source: Remarkably, anchorage of ERCs to NPCs results in the dissociation of their nuclear basket, which is a direct result of SAGA-driven acetylation of nucleoporins on the nucleoplasmic side of the NPC, including Nup60 (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Most of the NPCs of old yeast cells lack a nuclear basket.
source: Consequently, most of the NPCs of old yeast cells lack a nuclear basket (Meinema et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In many metazoans, including humans, aging results in an increasing frequency of chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, correlating with increasing risk of cancer.
source: In many metazoans, including humans, aging results in an increasing frequency of chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, correlating with increasing risk of cancer (Boveri, 2008; Jacobs et al., 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All young mother cells (~0–3 CBE; t=0 hr) and their daughters contained a fluorescent dot, documenting the presence of the labeled chromosomes in all of them.
source: Analysis of these images showed that all young mother cells (~0–3 CBE; t=0 hr) and their daughters contained a fluorescent dot, documenting the presence of the labeled chromosomes in all of them.
evidence: This claim is supported by the microscopy data presented in Figure 1.

claim: When reaching the age of 18–22 CBE (t=24 hr), 10–15% of old mother cells had lost their chromosome dot.
source: However, when reaching the age of 18–22 CBE (t=24 hr), 10–15% of these now old mother cells had lost their dot (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Chromosome dot loss was observed irrespective of which chromosome was labeled, and which fluorescent tag was used.
source: This was observed irrespective of which chromosome was labeled, and which fluorescent tag was used.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1C showing similar loss frequencies for different chromosomes and labeling methods.

claim: Fluorescence of the labeled SPB was not affected in old cells, indicating that dot loss was not caused by fluorophore instability.
source: Fluorescence of the labeled SPB was not affected, indicating that dot loss was not caused by fluorophore instability in old cells.
evidence: This is a control observation supporting the validity of the chromosome loss measurements.

claim: 85% of the cells lacking the TetO array had lost the LacO array, indicating they had lost the entire chromosome.
source: Analysis of these images showed that 85% of the cells lacking the TetO array had indeed lost the LacO array (50/59). Thus, these cells had probably lost the entire chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual-labeling experiments on chromosome IV.

claim: More than 99% (145/146 chromosome II loss events) of the dot-less cells failed to divide further, as expected for a haploid cell losing an entire chromosome.
source: Supporting this notion, loss of the TetO array was fatal to the cells. More than 99% (145/146 chromosome II loss events) of the dot-less cells failed to divide further, as expected for a haploid cell losing an entire chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct observation of cell fate after chromosome loss.

claim: Chromosome loss took place specifically in the last division of old mother cells and likely caused their death.
source: Thus, chromosome loss took place specifically in the last division of old mother cells and likely caused their death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells that lose chromosomes fail to divide further.

claim: The co-loss rate of both chromosome II and chromosome IV (~5%) was lower than the individual loss rates (~10–15%), but notably higher than the ~1% expected by chance alone.
source: As expected, the co-loss rate (~5%) was lower than the individual loss rates (~10–15%), but notably higher than the ~1% expected by chance alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dual chromosome loss events.

claim: 35–70% of aging mother cells likely lose several chromosomes in their final division, whereas the other cells die with an intact karyotype.
source: Considering that the budding yeast haploid genome has 16 chromosomes, the high loss frequency of a single chromosome and the fact that individual chromosomes are lost in not fully independent manners, we estimate that 35–70% of aging mother cells likely lose several chromosomes in their final division, whereas the other cells die with an intact karyotype.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the observed loss frequencies and statistical considerations.

claim: Extra-chromosomal DNA circles accumulate in the yeast mother cell with age rather than being lost.
source: In contrast to chromosomes, extra-chromosomal DNA circles accumulate in the yeast mother cell with age rather than being lost (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deleting the centromere from a chromosome causes the retention of both sister chromatids in the mother cell.
source: Similarly, deleting the centromere from a chromosome causes the retention of both sister chromatids in the mother cell (Kruitwagen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DNA circles containing a centromeric sequence (CEN) were lost from aged mother cells at a similar rate to full-size chromosomes (~20% of old cells).
source: DNA circles containing a centromeric sequence (CEN) were lost from aged mother cells at a similar rate to full-size chromosomes (~20% of old cells; Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Removing the centromere from a mini-chromosome causes its retention in the mother cell rather than its loss.
source: Removing the centromere of the exact same circle was shown in previous work to cause its retention in the mother cell rather than its loss (Meinema et al., 2022; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Centromeres are necessary and sufficient for chromosomes and mini chromosomes to be lost from aging mother cells.
source: Therefore, centromeres are necessary and sufficient for chromosomes and mini chromosomes to be lost from aging mother cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments with centromeric and non-centromeric DNA circles.

claim: Old mother cells lost mini-chromosomes expressing short-lived GFP at essentially the same frequency as they lost the TetO-labeled ones.
source: Scoring of the GFP signal demonstrated that old mother cells lost these mini-chromosomes at essentially the same frequency as they lost the TetO-labeled one (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing different labeling methods.

claim: There was a striking increase in the frequency of chromosome missegregation in old mother cells during anaphase.
source: Analysis of anaphases in old mother cells revealed a striking increase in the frequency of chromosome missegregation, using labeled chromosome II, IV, and minichromosome as reporters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In 600 total anaphase events, 66 (11%) co-segregated the labeled sister chromatids to a single pole with 54/66 (82%) resulting in asymmetric partition to the bud.
source: In 600 total anaphase events captured in our movies, we found that 66 (11%) of them co-segregated the labeled sister chromatids to a single pole with 54/66 (82%) of the missegregation events resulting in asymmetric partition of the chromatids to the bud of these old mother cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of anaphase events shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Asymmetric chromosome segregation to the bud was virtually never observed in young cells.
source: This was virtually never observed in young cells (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing young and old cells in Figure 2B.

claim: Chromosome loss from old mother cells is fully explained by a rise in sister chromatid non-disjunction with age, resulting in co-segregation of the sister chromatids asymmetrically to the bud.
source: Therefore, chromosome loss from old mother cells seems fully explained by a rise in sister chromatid non-disjunction with age, resulting in co-segregation of the sister chromatids asymmetrically to the bud.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative agreement between chromosome loss frequency and anaphase missegregation frequency.

claim: The pre-existing (old) SPB segregates in a highly biased manner to the bud (~95% of mitoses) in budding yeast.
source: In budding yeast, the pre-existing (old) SPB, which the cell inherited from the previous mitosis, segregates in a highly biased manner to the bud (~95% of mitoses) (Lengefeld et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2001; Hotz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In about 10% of old cells, SPB inheritance is inverted, meaning that the old SPB goes to the mother cell instead of the daughter.
source: In about 10% of old cells, SPB inheritance is inverted, meaning that the old SPB goes to the mother cell instead of the daughter (Lengefeld et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In 80% of cases where SPB inheritance was inverted, the non-disjoining sister chromatids followed the old SPB to the mother cell instead of going to the bud.
source: In a strong majority of these cases (80%), the non-disjoining sister chromatids followed the old SPB to the mother cell, instead of going to the bud (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E analyzing SPB-chromosome co-segregation.

claim: Non-disjoining sister chromatids of old mother cells remained attached to the pre-existing SPB and partitioned with it to the bud, causing them to lose these chromosomes.
source: We conclude that non-disjoining sister chromatids of old mother cells remained attached to the pre-existing SPB and partitioned with it to the bud, causing them to lose these chromosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of SPB-chromosome co-segregation patterns.

claim: In budding yeast, sister chromatids both initially attach to the pre-existing SPB, and these syntelic attachments are then dissolved by the aurora B kinase.
source: In budding yeast, sister chromatids both initially attach to the pre-existing SPB, which is available first. These syntelic attachments are then dissolved by the aurora B kinase, allowing sister chromatids to reorient, reach bi-orientation, and partition symmetrically in mitosis (Biggins et al., 1999; Cheeseman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing the error correction mechanism.

claim: Failure to correct initial attachment errors causes sister chromatids to co-segregate with the old SPB to the bud.
source: Failure to correct these initial attachment errors causes sister chromatids to co-segregate with the old SPB to the bud (Tanaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Young cells carrying the temperature-sensitive ipl1-321 mutant allele and grown at a permissive temperature (27 °C) showed no detectable chromosome loss.
source: Young cells carrying the temperature-sensitive ipl1-321 mutant allele and grown at a permissive temperature (27 °C) showed no detectable chromosome loss (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ipl1-321 mutant cells started losing chromosomes early in age, resulting in a shortened lifespan.
source: However, they started losing chromosomes early in age (Figure 2F), resulting in a shortened lifespan (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The chromosome loss frequency of the old ipl1-321 mutant cells (t=24 h) was indistinguishable from that of the wild-type cells, indicating that the effects of age and reducing Ipl1 activity were not additive.
source: Strikingly, the chromosome loss frequency of the old ipl1-321 mutant cells (t=24 h) was indistinguishable from that of the wild-type cells, indicating that the effects of age and reducing Ipl1 activity were not additive (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F comparing loss frequencies.

claim: Old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting chromosome attachment errors.
source: We concluded that old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting chromosome attachment errors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the non-additive effects of age and ipl1-321 mutation.

claim: Mutant cells lacking the deacetylase Sir2 form ERCs at an increased rate, accumulate them quicker, and their replicative lifespan is shorter than that of wild-type cells.
source: Mutant cells lacking the deacetylase Sir2, which inhibits recombination in the rDNA locus, form ERCs at an increased rate, accumulate them quicker, and their replicative lifespan is shorter than that of wild-type cells (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: sir2Δ mutant cells showed a strong and premature loss of the reporter chromosome.
source: Supporting the notion that ERC accumulation might promote chromosome loss, these mutant cells also showed a strong and premature loss of the reporter chromosome (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Removing replication fork barriers by inactivating the fork barrier protein Fob1 drastically decreases the rate at which ERCs form and accumulate, stabilizes the nuclear baskets of NPCs, and prolongs the life span of the cells.
source: Therefore, removing these fork barriers, for example, by inactivating the fork barrier protein Fob1, drastically decreases the rate at which ERCs form and accumulate, stabilizes the nuclear baskets of NPCs, and prolongs the life span of the cells (Meinema et al., 2022; Defossez et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: fob1Δ mutant cells lost chromosome II at a substantially reduced frequency compared to wild-type cells, even after dividing 20 times or more.
source: Strikingly, the fob1∆ mutant cells trapped in our microfluidics platform lost chromosome II at a substantially reduced frequency compared to wild-type cells, even after dividing 20 times or more (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Introducing an artificial replicative DNA circle with a different sequence than an ERC into wild-type cells promoted chromosome loss.
source: Introducing an artificial replicative DNA circle with a different sequence than an ERC into wild-type cells also promoted chromosome loss, supporting the idea that DNA circles promote chromosome loss with age independently of their sequence (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented later in the manuscript (Figure 6).

claim: Chromosome loss rates correlate well with the accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA circles.
source: Taken together, the chromosome loss rates seen in cells with artificial DNA circles, along with those in sir2∆ and fob1∆ cells, show that chromosome loss correlates well with the accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA circles.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on multiple genetic manipulations affecting ERC levels.

claim: Removal of the SAGA subunit Sgf73, which mediates ERC attachment to NPCs and the subsequent displacement of their nuclear basket, phenocopied the effect of the fob1Δ mutation.
source: Supporting this notion, removal of the SAGA subunit Sgf73, which mediates ERC attachment to NPCs and the subsequent displacement of their nuclear basket, phenocopied the effect of the fob1∆ mutation (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014): the sgf73∆ mutant cells failed to show any significant increase in chromosome loss frequency at any age (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citation to previous work on Sgf73 function.

claim: ERC formation and anchorage to NPCs triggered chromosome loss in old yeast cells.
source: Thus, our data suggested that ERC formation and anchorage to NPCs triggered chromosome loss in old yeast cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic experiments with sir2Δ, fob1Δ, and sgf73Δ mutants.

claim: mlp1Δ single mutant cells exhibited a rapid increase in chromosome loss frequency as they aged, along with a shortened replicative lifespan.
source: In stark contrast to the sgf73∆ and fob1∆ single mutants and the wild-type cells, the mlp1∆ single mutant cells exhibited a rapid increase in chromosome loss frequency as they aged, as determined by using our reporter chromosome II, along with a shortened replicative lifespan (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Displacement of the basket from NPCs as the cells age promotes chromosome loss through some yet unknown mechanism.
source: Thus, our data suggest that displacement of the basket from NPCs as the cells age promotes chromosome loss through some yet unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mlp1Δ phenotype.

claim: Only three genes involved in chromosome segregation contain an intron: NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
source: While perusing the list of genes involved in chromosome segregation (Figure 4A), we noticed that only three of them contain an intron, NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the yeast genome and is presented in Figure 4A.

claim: NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 all function with Ipl1/aurora B in preventing syntelic chromosome attachment.
source: Surprisingly, these three genes all function with Ipl1/aurora B in preventing syntelic chromosome attachment. Nbl1/borealin is a component of the chromosome passenger complex of which aurora B/Ipl1 is the catalytic subunit. Mcm21/CENP-O is a docking receptor for Ipl1/aurora B at kinetochores. Glc7/PP1A is the protein phosphatase 1, which counteracts aurora B by dephosphorylating its targets at the outer-kinetochore (Pinsky et al., 2006; Poddar et al., 1999; Nakajima et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing the functions of these proteins.

claim: Removing each intron individually or all three simultaneously (3 x∆i strain) had no detectable effects on chromosome segregation in young cells.
source: Removing each intron individually or all three simultaneously (3 x∆i strain) had no detectable effects on chromosome segregation in young cells (Figure 4B), cell growth and mitotic timing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Simultaneously removing all three introns nearly completely suppressed chromosome loss in old cells.
source: Simultaneously removing all three introns nearly completely suppressed chromosome loss in old cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Removing the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 individually or in pairs suppressed chromosome loss, albeit the effects were milder than removing all three.
source: Removing them individually or in pairs did so as well, albeit the effects were milder.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The simultaneous removal of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 introns did not affect the duration of the last budding event.
source: Importantly, the simultaneous removal of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 introns did not affect the duration of the last budding event (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), indicating that it suppressed chromosome loss without altering cell cycle progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Removing the introns of the two α-tubulin genes TUB1 and TUB3 simultaneously had no effect on chromosome loss.
source: Removing the introns of the two α-tubulin genes TUB1 and TUB3 simultaneously had no effect, indicating that the observed effects were specifically related to the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 and not to introns in general (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B as a negative control.

claim: The effects of removing the three introns were similar for chromosome II and chromosome IV, indicating that the role of these introns was not chromosome specific.
source: The effects observed were similar for chromosome II and chromosome IV, indicating that the role of these introns was not chromosome specific (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Removing the three introns also suppressed the occurrence of asymmetric anaphases in old cells.
source: Furthermore, removing these three introns also suppressed the occurrence of asymmetric anaphases in old cells (Figure 4C), supporting the view that asymmetric chromosome segregation and chromosome loss go hand-in-hand and are under the control of these three introns.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Removal of the three introns also suppressed chromosome loss in the ipl1-321 mutant cells.
source: Strengthening this conclusion, removal of these introns also suppressed chromosome loss in the ipl1-321 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Simultaneous removal of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7 introns extended replicative lifespan up to ~20%.
source: Remarkably, simultaneous removal of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7 introns also had a substantial effect on the longevity of the cells, extending their replicative lifespan up to ~20% (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A similar lifespan extension effect was observed in the ipl1-321 mutant cells upon intron removal.
source: A similar effect was observed in the ipl1-321 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chromosome loss may be the first direct cause of death for many yeast cells upon aging, although other mechanisms eventually take over when chromosome loss is abrogated.
source: Thus, chromosome loss may indeed be the first direct cause of death for many yeast cells upon aging, although other mechanisms eventually take over when chromosome loss is abrogated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial lifespan extension observed when chromosome loss is suppressed.

claim: mlp1Δ mutant cells exhibited a fourfold increase in their chromosome missegregation frequency compared to young wild-type cells.
source: Analysis of chromosome II segregation indicated that the mlp1∆ mutant cells not only exhibited a fourfold increase in their chromosome missegregation frequency compared to the young wild-type cells, but ~80% of these missegregation events followed the old SPB, as in old cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: ~80% of chromosome missegregation events in mlp1Δ mutant cells followed the old SPB, as in old cells.
source: Analysis of chromosome II segregation indicated that the mlp1∆ mutant cells not only exhibited a fourfold increase in their chromosome missegregation frequency compared to the young wild-type cells, but ~80% of these missegregation events followed the old SPB, as in old cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Chromosome loss in mlp1Δ mutant cells was suppressed upon removal of the introns of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7.
source: Furthermore, this chromosome loss was suppressed upon removal of the introns of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Defects in the nuclear basket result in asymmetric chromosome partitioning in an intron-dependent manner in young cells.
source: Therefore, although to a lower extent than in old cells, defects in the nuclear basket result in asymmetric chromosome partitioning in an intron-dependent manner in young cells as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mlp1Δ phenotype and its suppression by intron removal.

claim: Removal of the three introns rescued the age-dependent chromosome loss and partially restored the longevity of the mlp1Δ mutant cells.
source: Interestingly, removal of these three introns also rescued the age-dependent chromosome loss and partially restored the longevity of the mlp1∆ mutant cells (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Intron-dependent dampening of the error correction pathway is one, even if not the only progeric effects of the mlp1Δ mutation.
source: We concluded that intron-dependent dampening of the error correction pathway is one, even if not the only progeric effects of the mlp1∆ mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the partial rescue of mlp1Δ phenotypes by intron removal.

claim: Basket displacement promotes chromosome loss in young mutant cells and old wild-type mother cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that basket displacement promotes chromosome loss in young mutant cells and old wild-type mother cells.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the mlp1Δ and aging phenotypes.

claim: Cells carrying YRp17 showed a much shorter lifespan (10 CBE median RLS).
source: As expected (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997), the cells carrying YRp17 showed a much shorter lifespan (10 CBE median RLS, Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The effect of YRp17 on longevity was substantially suppressed by the 3 x∆i mutations.
source: Remarkably, however, the effect of YRp17 on longevity was substantially suppressed by the 3 x∆i mutations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Introducing YRp17 DNA circle promoted chromosome loss, starting early in life and increasing rapidly with age.
source: Analysis of chromosome loss indicated that introducing this DNA circle promoted chromosome loss, starting early in life and increasing rapidly with age (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Removal of the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 (3 x∆i cells) largely suppressed the effect of YRp17 on chromosome loss.
source: Furthermore, removal of the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 (3 x∆i cells) largely suppressed the effect of YRp17 on chromosome loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The suppressive effect of the 3 x∆i mutations on longevity and chromosome loss caused by YRp17 was only partial, indicating that YRp17 promotes chromosome loss through both a mechanism that involves these three introns, and at least one additional mechanism independent of these introns.
source: However, note that the suppressive effect of the 3 x∆i mutations on longevity and chromosome loss was only partial, indicating that YRp17 promotes chromosome loss through both a mechanism that involves these three introns, and at least one additional mechanism independent of these introns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial suppression observed.

claim: The 3 x∆i triple mutation significantly, though modestly, improved the longevity phenotype of sir2Δ mutant cells.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the 3 x∆i triple mutation significantly, though modestly, improved the longevity phenotype of these cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The triple intron removal ameliorated the premature chromosome loss phenotype of the sir2Δ mutant cells.
source: As in cells carrying YRp17, the triple intron removal indeed ameliorated the premature chromosome loss phenotype of the sir2∆ mutant cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The accumulation of DNA circles promotes the dissociation of the basket from NPCs and thereby drives chromosome loss at least in part through the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
source: Thus, we concluded that the accumulation of DNA circles, such as ERCs and others, which promote the dissociation of the basket from NPCs and thereby drive chromosome loss at least in part through the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the YRp17 and sir2Δ experiments.

claim: The effect of basket displacement on chromosome loss appeared to be the dominant one in physiologically aged cells, but additional effects seem to further promote chromosome loss in the sir2Δ mutant cells and cells carrying an exogenous DNA circle.
source: While this effect appeared to be the dominant one in physiologically aged cells, additional effects seem to further promote chromosome loss in the sir2∆ mutant cells and cells carrying an exogenous DNA circle, such as YRp17.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial suppression by intron removal in sir2Δ and YRp17 contexts.

claim: Basket mutant cells fail to retain unspliced pre-mRNAs in the nucleus.
source: Since basket mutant cells fail to retain unspliced pre-mRNAs in the nucleus (Galy et al., 2004; Bonnet and Palancade, 2015), we reasoned that old yeast mother cells also might leak pre-mRNAs to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the yeast genome, only 20 introns are longer than 500 nucleotides.
source: In the yeast genome, only 20 introns are longer than 500 nucleotides.
evidence: This is a statement about the yeast genome structure.

claim: With each of the three intron probes (DBP2, YRA1, GLC7), one or two nuclear foci were detected in young cells, and only very few cells (<3%) showed a focus in the cytoplasm.
source: With each of these three series of smRNA FISH probes, we detected one or two nuclear foci in young cells (Figure 7A). Only very few cells (<3%) showed a focus in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA FISH data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: No smRNA FISH foci were detected upon deleting the corresponding introns (∆i), demonstrating probe specificity.
source: No foci were detected upon deleting the corresponding introns (∆i), demonstrating probe specificity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by control data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: For each of the three introns tested, smRNA FISH detected intronic RNA sequences in the cytoplasm of most old cells.
source: In contrast, for each of the three introns tested, smRNA FISH detected intronic RNA sequences in the cytoplasm of most old cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA FISH data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: ~70% of GLC7 smRNA FISH foci were found in the cytoplasm of old mother cells, compared to ~3% in young cells.
source: For example, in the case of GLC7, ~70% of smRNA FISH foci were found in the cytoplasm of old mother cells, compared to ~3% in young cells (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 3 out of 3 tested introns showed a strong tendency to leak to the cytoplasm in old mother cells.
source: Thus, 3 out of 3 tested introns showed a strong tendency to leak to the cytoplasm in old mother cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the smRNA FISH results.

claim: The mCherry/GFP ratio of the pre-mRNA translation reporter increased in old compared to young cells, demonstrating elevated pre-mRNA translation in the cytoplasm of a large majority of aged cells.
source: Fluorescence signal analysis established that the mCherry/GFP ratio increased in old compared to young cells, demonstrating elevated pre-mRNA translation in the cytoplasm of a large majority of aged cells (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-E using the pre-mRNA translation reporter.

claim: The mCherry/GFP ratio increased prematurely and to a higher level in the sir2Δ mutant, compared to the wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with ERC-dependent leakage and translation of this reporter, the mCherry/GFP ratio increased prematurely and to a higher level in the sir2∆ mutant, compared to the wild-type cells (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: The fob1Δ mutant cells showed a lowered mCherry/GFP ratio, which did not increase much during their lifespan.
source: Conversely, the fob1∆ mutant cells showed a lowered mCherry/GFP ratio, which did not increase much during their lifespan (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: ERC formation and accumulation promote pre-mRNA leakage during yeast aging.
source: Thus, we conclude that ERC formation and accumulation promote pre-mRNA leakage during yeast aging, as expected from their effect on the nuclear basket.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pre-mRNA reporter data in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: The two yeast SR-proteins Gbp2 and Hrb1 have been implicated in the retention of pre-mRNAs in the nucleus by binding intron-containing transcripts and delaying their export until they are properly spliced or degraded.
source: The two yeast SR-proteins Gbp2 and Hrb1 have been implicated in the retention of pre-mRNAs in the nucleus by binding intron-containing transcripts and delaying their export until they are properly spliced or degraded (Hackmann et al., 2014; Hurt et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells leak pre-mRNA to the cytoplasm at a higher rate than wild-type cells.
source: Accordingly, the hrb1∆ gbp2∆ double mutant cells leak pre-mRNA to the cytoplasm at a higher rate than wild-type cells (Hackmann et al., 2014; Windgassen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Young spliceosome-defective snu66Δ mutant cells exhibited a fivefold elevated level of chromosome missegregation compared to young wild-type cells.
source: The young spliceosome-defective snu66∆ mutant cells did exhibit a fivefold elevated level of chromosome missegregation compared to young wild-type cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Chromosome missegregation in snu66Δ mutant cells was not biased towards any specific SPB.
source: However, this missegregation was not biased towards any specific SPB (Figure 8A–B), suggesting that it involved a distinct mechanism than that observed in old cells and in young cells lacking the basket protein Mlp1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells showed a more than 10-fold increased frequency of chromosome missegregation compared to young wild-type cells.
source: In contrast to the snu66∆ mutant, the hrb1∆ gbp2∆ double mutant cells showed an even further increased frequency of chromosome missegregation, which was more than 10-fold above that of young wild-type cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Sister chromatid missegregation in hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells was strongly biased towards the old SPB.
source: Furthermore, sister chromatid missegregation was strongly biased towards the old SPB (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Removing the introns of GLC7, MCM21, and NBL1 suppressed the chromosome segregation defect in hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells.
source: Removing the introns of GLC7, MCM21, and NBL1 suppressed this chromosome segregation defect (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Pre-mRNA leakage is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome partitioning and is contingent on the presence of introns in the error correction genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
source: Therefore, pre-mRNA leakage is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome partitioning and is contingent on the presence of introns in the error correction genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hrb1Δ gbp2Δ phenotype and its suppression by intron removal.

claim: Mutations affecting the spliceosome did not promote asymmetric chromosome segregation to any specific SPB with age, indicating that the chromosome loss observed in old cells is not due to splicing defects.
source: The fact that mutations affecting the spliceosome did not promote asymmetric chromosome segregation to any specific SPB with age indicates that the chromosome loss observed in old cells is not due to splicing defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between snu66Δ and hrb1Δ gbp2Δ phenotypes.

claim: The accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA causes the displacement of the NPC basket and subsequent leakage of pre-mRNAs.
source: We conclude that the accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA causes the displacement of the NPC basket and subsequent leakage of pre-mRNAs.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the entire set of experiments.

claim: Leakage of intron-containing transcripts into the cytoplasm impairs correction of syntelic attachments by the Ipl1/aurora B pathway.
source: Leakage of intron-containing transcripts into the cytoplasm impairs correction of syntelic attachments by the Ipl1/aurora B pathway, likely because three genes involved in this pathway contain introns.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the convergence of all experimental results.

claim: Impaired error correction results in asymmetric partitioning of sister chromatids and age-associated chromosome loss.
source: This results in asymmetric partitioning of sister chromatids and age-associated chromosome loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion linking the molecular mechanism to the phenotype.

claim: Basket displacement and pre-mRNA leakage impair error correction via an as-yet unknown mechanism involving the introns of NBL1, MCM21 and GLC7.
source: In summary, basket displacement and pre-mRNA leakage impair error correction via an as-yet unknown mechanism involving the introns of NBL1, MCM21 and GLC7.
evidence: This is a summary statement acknowledging that the precise molecular mechanism remains to be determined.

claim: NPC remodelling is both necessary and sufficient to drive the age-associated increase in chromosome loss.
source: We showed that NPC remodelling is both necessary and sufficient to drive the age-associated increase in chromosome loss and we identified the mechanisms involved.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the genetic experiments showing that preventing NPC remodeling suppresses chromosome loss and promoting it induces chromosome loss.

claim: Interventions that promoted displacement of the NPC basket, or basket defects more broadly, enhanced non-disjunction and missegregation of sister chromatids to the bud, thereby promoting chromosome loss in old yeast cells.
source: Specifically, interventions that promoted displacement of the NPC basket, or basket defects more broadly, enhanced non-disjunction and missegregation of sister chromatids to the bud, thereby promoting chromosome loss in old yeast cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results with sir2Δ and mlp1Δ mutants.

claim: Interventions that prevented NPC remodelling restored proper chromosome segregation in old cells and suppressed chromosome loss.
source: Conversely, interventions that prevented NPC remodelling, such as delaying ERC accumulation or preventing their anchorage and the recruitment of SAGA to NPCs, restored proper chromosome segregation in old cells and suppressed chromosome loss.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results with fob1Δ and sgf73Δ mutants.

claim: NPC remodeling is the pivotal point for triggering chromosome loss in old cells.
source: Thus, NPC remodeling appeared to be the pivotal point for triggering chromosome loss in old cells.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on all the genetic and mechanistic data.

claim: The sir2Δ and fob1Δ mutations each have effects beyond influencing ERC formation rates.
source: First, the sir2∆ and fob1∆ mutations each have effects beyond influencing ERC formation rates.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential confounding factors in the interpretation.

claim: The only clear common denominator between sir2Δ and fob1Δ mutations is that they both affect ERC formation, and hence NPC remodelling, even if in opposite manners.
source: However, their only clear common denominator is that they both affect ERC formation, and hence NPC remodelling, even if in opposite manners (Kaeberlein et al., 1999; Defossez et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an argument supporting the causal role of ERC-mediated NPC remodeling.

claim: The only known functional overlap between Fob1 and Sgf73 is that they promote ERC accumulation in the mother cell indirectly (Fob1) or directly (Sgf73), ERC anchorage to NPCs, and the consequent displacement of NPC basket.
source: Here again, the only known functional overlap between Fob1 and Sgf73 is that they promote ERC accumulation in the mother cell indirectly (Fob1) or directly (Sgf73), ERC anchorage to NPCs, and the consequent displacement of NPC basket (Meinema et al., 2022; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an argument supporting the causal role of ERC-mediated NPC remodeling.

claim: DNA circle accumulation and attachment to NPCs trigger chromosome loss.
source: Thus, our data establish that DNA circle accumulation and attachment to NPCs trigger chromosome loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the convergence of multiple lines of genetic evidence.

claim: Destabilizing the basket independently of DNA circle accumulation promotes the premature onset of chromosome loss.
source: Destabilizing the basket independently of DNA circle accumulation also promotes the premature onset of chromosome loss, indicating that it is the basket displacement from NPCs that triggers chromosome loss upon DNA circle accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mlp1Δ phenotype.

claim: Chromosome loss is due to the non-correction of syntelic chromosome attachments in old cells.
source: Our data reveal that chromosome loss is due to the non-correction of syntelic chromosome attachments in old cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the SPB co-segregation data and ipl1-321 experiments.

claim: The inhibition of error correction in old cells requires the presence of three introns, those of the genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
source: Our data also show that the inhibition of error correction in old cells requires the presence of three introns, those of the genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the intron removal experiments.

claim: NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 are the only chromosome segregation machinery genes that contain an intron.
source: These three genes are the only chromosome segregation machinery genes that contain an intron.
evidence: This is based on genome analysis presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Removing the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 restored proper attachment correction and chromosome segregation in old cells.
source: Removing their introns restored proper attachment correction and chromosome segregation in old cells and suppressed the premature chromosome loss phenotype of the ipl1-321 mutant cells grown at semi-permissive temperature.
evidence: This is a summary of the intron removal effects.

claim: Intron removal delays cell death but does not abrogate aging.
source: Intron removal delays cell death but does not abrogate aging.
evidence: This is based on the observation that lifespan is extended but not indefinitely.

claim: Removing the three introns not only suppresses chromosome missegregation in old wild-type cells, but also in young mlp1Δ mutant cells.
source: Furthermore, removing these introns not only suppresses chromosome missegregation in old wild-type cells, but also in young mlp1∆ mutant cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the intron removal effects across different contexts.

claim: Intron removal separates aging and chromosome loss, indicating that these introns are part of the proximal cause of chromosome loss and act independently of age.
source: Thus, intron removal separates aging and chromosome loss, indicating that these introns are part of the proximal cause of chromosome loss and act independently of age.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that intron removal suppresses chromosome loss without preventing aging.

claim: There is a direct, intron-dependent link between basket displacement from NPCs and chromosome loss.
source: Therefore, our data indicate that there is a direct, intron-dependent link between basket displacement from NPCs and chromosome loss.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: The link between basket displacement and chromosome loss involves the leakage of unspliced pre-mRNAs out of the nucleus upon basket removal and affects the basket's function in mRNA quality control.
source: Our data indicate that this link involves the leakage of unspliced pre-mRNAs out of the nucleus upon basket removal and affects the basket's function in mRNA quality control.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the pre-mRNA leakage data and the intron-dependence of the phenotype.

claim: The fact that hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells also increase the frequency of chromosome loss through the same three introns strengthens the conclusion that pre-mRNA leakage causes chromosome loss.
source: The fact that another independent set of mutations that also interfere with pre-mRNA retention in the nucleus, such as the gbp2∆ hrb1∆ double mutant cells, also increases the frequency of chromosome loss through the same three introns strengthens this conclusion.
evidence: This is an argument supporting the causal role of pre-mRNA leakage.

claim: Displacement of the nuclear basket from NPCs in old mother cells directly triggers chromosome non-disjunction and loss through causing the leakage of the pre-mRNAs of the intron-containing genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
source: Thus, together our data establish that displacement of the nuclear basket from NPCs in old mother cells directly triggers chromosome non-disjunction and loss through causing the leakage of the pre-mRNAs of the intron-containing genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study.

claim: Basket displacement could affect many more cellular functions than only chromosome segregation.
source: First, it means that NPC remodelling could affect many more cellular functions than only chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the broad functions of the nuclear basket.

claim: Beyond mRNA quality control, the basket of the NPC is also involved in protein quality control and the activation of environmentally regulated genes, two processes that are impaired in old cells.
source: Interestingly, beyond mRNA quality control, the basket of the NPC is also involved in protein quality control and the activation of environmentally regulated genes, two processes that are impaired in old cells (Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; López-Otín et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Basket displacement might contribute to protein quality control and gene activation defects in aging cells.
source: Thus, basket displacement might contribute to these phenotypes in aging cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known functions of the basket.

claim: The role of the basket in mRNA quality control could affect more than only chromosome segregation.
source: It is also very likely that the role of the basket in mRNA quality control could affect more than only chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a speculation about broader implications.

claim: Introns in budding yeast are enriched in very specific processes, such as genes coding for ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes and proteasome subunits, components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, and ribosomal proteins.
source: Curiously, while budding yeasts have kept only a subset of the introns of their ancestors, these introns are not distributed randomly and seem to be enriched in very specific processes, such as genes coding for ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes and proteasome subunits, components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, and ribosomal proteins (Lim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Decay of the ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ribosome assembly are classical and ubiquitous hallmarks of aging.
source: Interestingly, decay of the ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ribosome assembly are classical and ubiquitous hallmarks of aging (Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; López-Otín et al., 2023; Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is possible that basket displacement in old cells contributes to the emergence of aging phenotypes related to protein degradation, mitochondrial function, and ribosome assembly.
source: Thus, it is possible that basket displacement in old cells contributes to the emergence of these aging phenotypes as well.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the enrichment of introns in genes related to these processes.

claim: Displacement of the NPCs' basket is also observed in stressed cells and not solely in the context of aging.
source: A second type of consequences emerging from our observations stems from the fact that displacement of the NPCs' basket is also observed in stressed cells and not solely in the context of aging.
evidence: This is based on previous observations in the field.

claim: Heat shock causes basket displacement in yeast.
source: For example, heat shock also causes basket displacement in yeast (Carmody et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is possible that the downstream effects of basket displacement observed in old cells also take place during stress response.
source: Therefore, it is possible that the downstream effects we observe in old cells also take place during stress response.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that basket displacement occurs in both contexts.

claim: Heat shock has been associated with a strong rise in aneuploidy in yeast.
source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that heat shock has been associated with a strong rise in aneuploidy in yeast (Yona et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aneuploidy is a common response to environmental stress and a primary mechanism for the emergence of stress-resistant clones in fungi.
source: Furthermore, aneuploidy is a common response to environmental stress and a primary mechanism for the emergence of stress-resistant clones in fungi (Gilchrist and Stelkens, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that the chromosome missegregation resulting from basket displacement might be a selected response to stress.
source: Therefore, it is tempting to speculate that the chromosome missegregation resulting from basket displacement might be a selected response to stress.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary significance of the mechanism.

claim: It might be selectively advantageous for cells to actively promote karyotype variations when their survival is in question.
source: It might be selectively advantageous for cells to actively promote karyotype variations when their survival is in question.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary advantage.

claim: It is worth considering that a similar process, perhaps using similar mechanisms, underlies the aneuploidy of cancer cells.
source: It is therefore worth considering that a similar process, perhaps using similar mechanisms, underlies the aneuploidy of cancer cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about the relevance to cancer biology.

claim: The role of basket displacement in the emergence of aging phenotypes is likely not a peculiarity of yeast.
source: Third, the role of basket displacement in the emergence of aging phenotypes is likely not a peculiarity of yeast.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary conservation.

claim: Using proteomics, basket displacement has been inferred to take place in aging cells such as the hepatocytes of old mice and humans.
source: Using proteomics, basket displacement has been inferred to take place in aging cells such as the hepatocytes of old mice and humans (Ori et al., 2015; Malik et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intron retention is one of the hallmarks of aging on the metazoan transcriptome.
source: Little is known about whether the nuclear basket of metazoans plays a similar role in pre-mRNA retention in the nucleus as that of yeast, but it is striking that intron retention is one of the hallmarks of aging on the metazoan transcriptome, and that pre-mRNA processing genes are important for mitotic stability (Mariotti et al., 2022; Adusumalli et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2022; Funk et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pre-mRNA processing genes are important for mitotic stability.
source: Little is known about whether the nuclear basket of metazoans plays a similar role in pre-mRNA retention in the nucleus as that of yeast, but it is striking that intron retention is one of the hallmarks of aging on the metazoan transcriptome, and that pre-mRNA processing genes are important for mitotic stability (Mariotti et al., 2022; Adusumalli et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2022; Funk et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The most ubiquitous effect of the expression of the progeric variant of lamin A, progerin, across cell types is the displacement of the nuclear basket protein TPR from NPCs.
source: More strikingly, perhaps the most ubiquitous effect of the expression of the progeric variant of lamin A, progerin, across cell types is the displacement of the nuclear basket protein TPR from NPCs (Larrieu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Basket displacement might be relevant to the aetiology of the Gilford-Hutchinson Progeria Syndrome.
source: We know still very little about the impact of basket displacement in the aetiology of the Gilford-Hutchinson Progeria Syndrome, but our study suggests that it might be relevant.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in yeast and the known effects of progerin.

claim: Investigating the potential effects of progerin on pre-mRNA leakage might become an essential step towards understanding how progerin expression causes premature aging.
source: If so, investigating the potential effects of progerin on pre-mRNA leakage might become an essential step towards understanding how progerin expression causes premature aging.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: The effect of ERCs on NPCs may close the gap between ERC-driven aging in yeast and other aging processes in other eukaryotes.
source: For decades, the role of ERCs in aging has been perceived as a yeast peculiarity. However, the effect it has on NPCs may close the gap.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: The basket-centric view of aging would explain how ERCs actually cause aging in yeast and indicate that while ERC accumulation might be a yeast idiosyncrasy, its downstream effects are not.
source: Indeed, the basket-centric view of aging that we propose here would explain how ERCs actually cause aging in yeast and indicate that while ERC accumulation might be a yeast idiosyncrasy, its downstream effects are not.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary conservation of the mechanism.

claim: ERCs and any replicating eccDNA are the closest mimics that laboratory yeast strain may encounter of pathogenic DNA of exogenous origin.
source: We are intrigued by the idea that ERCs and any replicating eccDNA for that matter are the closest mimics that laboratory yeast strain may encounter of pathogenic DNA of exogenous origin.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary origin of the response.

claim: Basket displacement and the ensuing effects might have first appeared as a response to infections.
source: In that perspective, basket displacement and the ensuing effects might have first appeared as a response to infections.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary origin of the mechanism.

claim: Yeast aging might reflect the activity of a death pathway that normally functions in pathogen control, representing a fungal version of the inflammatory or auto-immune response in metazoans.
source: In other words, yeast aging might reflect the activity of a death pathway that normally functions in pathogen control. It might represent a fungal version of the inflammatory or auto-immune response in metazoans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary and functional significance of the mechanism.

claim: It will be interesting to investigate whether exogenous or non-chromosomal DNA, such as that of viruses, also triggers the displacement of the nuclear basket from NPCs in yeast and other systems.
source: Therefore, it will be interesting to investigate whether exogenous or non-chromosomal DNA, such as that of viruses, also triggers the displacement of the nuclear basket from NPCs in yeast and other systems, and whether this contributes to either or both of anti-viral defence and aging.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: If exogenous DNA triggers basket displacement, aging might have emerged as an anti-viral defence.
source: If so, aging might have emerged as an anti-viral defence.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary origin of aging.
